content: Artemether is rapidly metabolized into its active metabolite, dihydroartemisinin (DHA). The antimalarial activity of both artemether and DHA is attributed to the endoperoxide moiety present in their chemical structure. However, the precise mechanism by which lumefantrine exerts its antimalarial effects is not fully understood. Available evidence suggests that lumefantrine inhibits the formation of β-hematin by forming a complex with hemin. Both artemether and lumefantrine have been shown to inhibit nucleic acid and protein synthesis. Pharmacodynamics There is limited information available regarding the pharmacodynamics of artemether and lumefantrine in the drug label. Pharmacokinetics Absorption After oral administration of artemether/lumefantrine tablets to healthy volunteers and malaria patients, artemether is absorbed with peak plasma concentrations occurring approximately 2 hours post-dosing. Lumefantrine, being highly lipophilic, exhibits a lag time of up to 2 hours before absorption begins, with peak plasma concentrations reached approximately 6 to 8 hours after administration. The pharmacokinetic parameters for artemether, DHA (its active metabolite), and lumefantrine following a single dose (4 tablets) in healthy adult Caucasian volunteers are documented. Data from multiple doses after a 6-dose regimen in adult malaria patients are also available. Food significantly enhances the absorption of both artemether and lumefantrine. In healthy volunteers, the relative bioavailability of artemether increased by 2to 3-fold, and that of lumefantrine increased 16-fold when the tablets were taken after a high-fat meal compared to fasting conditions. Patients should be encouraged to take artemether/lumefantrine tablets with food as soon as they can tolerate it. Distribution Artemether and DHA are bound to human plasma proteins at rates of 95.4% and 47-76%, respectively. Protein binding is linear across the therapeutic range. Biotransformation In human liver microsomes and recombinant CYP450 enzymes, artemether metabolism is primarily catalyzed by CYP3A4/CYP3A5, with minor contributions from CYP2B6, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19. DHA is the active metabolite of artemether. In vitro studies at therapeutic concentrations revealed no significant inhibition of the metabolic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2A6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, CYP3A4/CYP3A5, or CYP4A9/3A11. Similarly, no significant induction of CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, or CYP3A5 was observed with artemether, DHA, or lumefantrine. During repeated administration of artemether/lumefantrine tablets, systemic exposure to artemether decreased significantly, while DHA concentrations increased, though not to a statistically significant degree. This suggests enzyme induction responsible for artemether metabolism. Lumefantrine is metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 to desbutyl-lumefantrine, with systemic exposure to the metabolite being less than 1% of the parent compound. In vitro, lumefantrine significantly inhibits CYP2D6 activity at therapeutic plasma concentrations. Co-administration of artemether/lumefantrine with CYP2D6 substrates may increase plasma concentrations of the substrates, raising the risk of adverse reactions. Elimination Artemether and DHA are cleared from plasma with an elimination half-life of approximately 2 hours. Lumefantrine is eliminated more slowly, with a half-life of 3 to 6 days in both healthy volunteers and patients with falciparum malaria. Demographic factors such as sex and weight do not appear to have clinically relevant effects on the pharmacokinetics of artemether and lumefantrine. Pharmacokinetics in Special Populations Hepatic and Renal Impairment No specific pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in patients with hepatic or renal impairment. There is no significant renal excretion of lumefantrine, artemether, or DHA in healthy volunteers. While clinical experience in this population is limited, no dose adjustment is recommended for patients with renal impairment. Pediatric Patients Pharmacokinetic data for artemether, DHA, and lumefantrine in pediatric patients were obtained from two studies using sparse sampling and a population-based approach. Systemic exposure to these compounds, when dosed on a mg/kg body weight basis in pediatric patients (5 to <35 kg body weight), is comparable to that observed in adults receiving the recommended dosing regimen. Geriatric Patients No specific pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in patients older than 65 years of age. Nonclinical Toxicology Carcinogenesis Carcinogenicity studies have not been conducted for the artemether/lumefantrine combination. Mutagenesis No evidence of mutagenicity was detected in studies evaluating the artemether/lumefantrine combination. These studies included the Salmonella and Escherichia/mammalian-microsome mutagenicity test, the gene mutation test with Chinese hamster cells (V79), the cytogenetic test on Chinese hamster cells in vitro, and the rat micronucleus test in vivo.
